Theme

Money, work & business · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

borrow verb

also borrowing, borrow money, can I borrow, may I borrow, hit someone for a loan, may I hit you for a loan?, touch someone for money

classical

Cic. Att. 7.3.11: ā Caeliō mūtuābimur, we’ll borrow from Caelius
Cic. Att. 15.15.3: cōgor mūtuārī, I am forced to borrow
Traupman 27

mūtuor, mūtuārī, mūtuātus sum

verb, first conjugation, deponent · Conjugation on Wiktionary

borrow (money)

Of money above all; also of words or ideas taken from another (Quint. 1.5.58: sīcut illī ā nōbīs nōnnumquam mūtuantur, as they sometimes borrow from us).

Other words

  • ūtendum petere — ask to borrow, borrow (a thing, to use and give back)

    verb phrase: the gerundive agrees with the thing borrowed · classical · Plaut. Aul. 400: artoptam ex proximō ūtendam petō; Cato Agr. 5.4: unde ūtenda roget

    Also ūtendum rogāre (Cato); to lend a thing so is ūtendum dare (Plaut. Asin. 444).

  • pecūniam mūtuam sūmere — borrow money, take a loan

    verb phrase · also used · classical · Caes. BC 1.39.3: ā tribūnīs mīlitum centuriōnibusque mūtuās pecūniās sūmpsit; Cic. Phil. 10.26: pecūniāsque … mūtuās sūmat

  • ferīre (aliquem) — hit (someone) for money, touch for a loan

    feriō, fourth conjugation, with the person as object; Traupman adds mūtuō (argentō) · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 1.1.13 (Lewis & Short), s.v. feriō: “to cozen, cheat, gull, trick (mostly in vulg. lang.; not in Cic.)”; Traupman 100, 102: ferīre aliquem mūtuō argentō; licet tē mūtuō ferīre?; Traupman 328 · Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

    Comic slang, “to strike” someone for money; it leans to fleecing rather than honest borrowing. The plain way is mūtuārī.

Examples

  • 'solvāmus' inquis. age, ā Caeliō mūtuābimur.

    ‘Let’s pay,’ you say. All right, we’ll borrow from Caelius.Cic. Att. 7.3.11

  • ego hinc artoptam ex proximō ūtendam petō ā Congriōne.

    I’ll go and borrow a bread-pan from next door, from Congrio.Plaut. Aul. 400–401

  • Duās aut trēs familiās habeat, unde ūtenda roget et quibus det, praetereā nēminī.

    Let him have two or three households to borrow things from and to lend them to, and no one else.Cato Agr. 5.4

See also loan, lend, give back, owe, debt.
